newsitem.title: SPAIN: Tighter EMU belt pinches popularity of Spain's PP.
newsitem.headline: Tighter EMU belt pinches popularity of Spain's PP.

text.p: Spain's conservative government felt the first pinch of its financial belt-tightening measures on Wednesday when an opinion poll showed a sharp drop in the Popular Party's popularity six months after coming to power.

The opposition Socialists, who lost a March election by 1.5 percentage points after ruling nearly 14 years, moved back into favour with a three-point lead over the conservatives in the government-sponsored poll presented to parliament on Wednesday.
"There's a certain erosion of the government's image," said Pilar del Castillo, director of the CIS polling unit.
"There's always been an awareness that the measures taken to comply with (European Monetary Union) convergence requirements could have this type of corrosive effect," she told journalists.
The October survey of 2,500 Spaniards found the Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) led the Popular Party (PP) by 3.6 points (39.9 against 36.3 percent) in voter intention.
The last poll measuring voter intention in July had the PP leading by about one percent. Other political parties maintained their levels of popularity.

More than half of those surveyed opposed the government's plan to freeze public sector salaries for two years, one of several strict measures in the 1997 draft budget aimed at getting Spain ready to join the single currency in 1999.
But a majority said they approved of the government's intention -- to reduce public spending.

Deputy Prime Minister Alvarez Cascos shrugged off the survey results as "normal", saying the government had adopted unpopular measures that would in the medium term have a good effect on the economy with a corresponding increase in public confidence.
The PP's general coordinator, Angel Acebes, said there was plenty of time in a four-year term for the party to recover in the public opinion.
